unit.title: Choosing where to invest
unit.description: Safe brokers, fees, neobrokers and robo-advisers: how to compare without falling into traps

steps.title: First, make sure it's safe
steps.body:
1. **Regulation:** authorised by the CNMV or by an EU supervisor with a **passport** to operate in Spain. Check on cnmv.es, not on its website.
2. **Protection:** your securities are yours and kept separate from the broker's own assets. If anything went missing, **FOGAIN** (Spain's investor compensation scheme) covers up to **€100,000** per investor at member firms. It doesn't cover market falls.

steps.title: Then, make sure it fits
steps.body:
3. **Costs:** buying and selling, custody, currency exchange, inactivity.
4. **Products:** does it have the index funds and ETFs you want?
5. **Tax:** **Spanish** brokers withhold tax and report to Hacienda (Spain's tax authority); **foreign** ones usually don't, so you declare everything yourself and maybe Modelo 720 too. Compensation schemes in other countries may have lower limits.

steps.title: What to take away
steps.body: A cheap but unauthorised broker is the most expensive of all: you could lose everything.
steps.key: First, make sure it's safe and authorised; then, that it's cheap.
steps.tip: Before looking at what a broker charges, look at who supervises it.

steps.title: What they charge you
steps.body:
• **Trading:** per trade (flat, percentage or mixed).
• **Custody:** for holding your securities, sometimes monthly or yearly.
• **Currency exchange:** when you buy in another currency. It's usually the **biggest hidden cost**: from 0.1 % to 0.5 % or more per trade.
• **Others:** inactivity, withdrawals, collecting dividends.

And inside every fund or ETF, its TER.

steps.title: Small things compound
steps.body: Try how the result changes over 20 or 30 years with 0.3 % more or less a year.
steps.tip: Always compare the total cost against the way you invest.

steps.title: It depends on how you invest
steps.body: A flat €3 fee is a bargain on a €10,000 purchase (0.03 %) and outrageous on a €100 one (3 %). If you put in small amounts each month, look for low percentage fees or no minimum; for a few large purchases, a flat fee can work out better.
steps.key: The cheapest broker is the one that charges you the least, given the way you invest.

steps.title: If it's free, who's paying?
steps.body:
Neobrokers (apps with €0 or near-zero trading) make money in other ways:

• **Payment for order flow (PFOF):** a market maker pays them to send it your orders.
• **Spread** and **currency exchange**.
• **Interest** on cash they don't pay you anything on.
• **Securities lending** of your shares.
• Premium **subscriptions**, crypto and CFDs.

steps.title: The rules in the EU
steps.body:
The EU's MiFIR regulation (2024) **bans payment for order flow** for retail clients. Some countries where it already existed were allowed to keep it as an exception **until 30 June 2026**.

On top of that, many apps use game design: confetti, notifications, streaks. The more you trade, the more they earn.

steps.title: What to take away
steps.body: An authorised neobroker can be a good cheap option. Just be clear about how it makes money and don't let the app decide how much you trade.
steps.key: When something is free, ask yourself how the people giving it to you make money.
steps.tip: If the app nudges you to trade every day, remember your plan is a 20-year one.

steps.title: What a robo-adviser is
steps.body:
An **automated portfolio management** service: you fill in a questionnaire (the **suitability test**), it assigns you a portfolio of index funds based on your profile and takes care of investing and **rebalancing** for you.

In Spain it has to be a firm authorised by the CNMV.

steps.title: How much it costs
steps.body: They usually charge a management fee plus the cost of the funds: in total, often between **0.4 % and 1 %** a year. More than doing it yourself with index funds (≈ 0.1-0.3 %), less than many active bank funds (1.5 % or more).

steps.title: You or the robot?
steps.body: Doing it yourself is cheaper if you're disciplined. A robo-adviser makes sense if it saves you from mistakes: forgetting to rebalance or panic selling. What it doesn't do is remove risk: if the market falls, your portfolio falls.
steps.key: A robo-adviser automates discipline, but it charges for it and doesn't remove market risk.

s11boss.title: Final challenge: Spain: taxes and scams

u33l1-1.prompt: Put the criteria for choosing a broker in order, from the first to the last you should look at.
u33l1-1.explanation: Safety first; price and convenience after.

u33l1-2.prompt: What do you check before opening an account? Select all that apply.
options: Its trading, custody and currency fees
How many followers it has on social media
That it's authorised in the CNMV registers
u33l1-2.explanation: Popularity on social media says nothing about how safe it is.

u33l1-3.prompt: What's the first thing you should check about a broker?
options: That it has the nicest app
That it's authorised by the CNMV or by a European supervisor with a passport
Up to €100,000 if a member firm can't return your money or securities
Everything you invest, with no limit
Losses when the stock market falls
u33l1-4.explanation: It protects you against the firm failing, not against how the market performs.

u33l1-5.prompt: A foreign broker usually withholds tax for you and sends your details to Hacienda.
u33l1-5.explanation: Usually not: it's up to you to declare every trade, and maybe file Modelo 720.

u33l1-6.prompt: A broker that doesn't appear in the CNMV registers offers you zero fees and a 100 % bonus on your first deposit. What do you do?
options: Rule it out: if it isn't authorised, there's nothing to compare
Try with a small amount and, if it goes well, put in more
Grab the bonus, it's free money
u33l1-6.explanation: Without authorisation, zero fees could cost you everything.
feedback: Good: the first filter is authorisation. Fees come afterwards.
Many scams let you win at first so that you put in more.
Bonuses are the typical bait, and without authorisation you have no protection at all.

u33l1-7.prompt: Is it more typical of a Spanish broker or a foreign one?
options: It may require you to file Modelo 720
Your income tax return comes almost ready-made
You have to declare every trade yourself
It withholds 19 % and sends your details to Hacienda
u33l1-7.explanation: Tax convenience also counts when comparing.
right: Spanish broker
Foreign broker

u33l1-8.prompt: FOGAIN covers up to ____ € per investor.
u33l1-8.explanation: If a member firm can't return your money or securities.

u33l1-9.prompt: Your shares and ETFs are kept separate from the broker's own assets.
u33l1-9.explanation: They're yours: if the broker goes bust, they should be returned to you.

u33l1-10.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u33l1-10.explanation: Four words that help you judge a broker.
right: Scheme that pays out if a firm doesn't return what's yours
Permission to operate in Spain while being authorised in another EU country
Return declaring securities and accounts held abroad
Supervisor of investment services in Spain

u33l2-1.prompt: You pay a flat €5 fee to buy €100 of an ETF. What percentage goes on the fee?
u33l2-1.explanation: 5 ÷ 100 = 5 %. You'd have to make 5 % just to break even.

u33l2-2.prompt: You buy €2,000 of US shares and the broker charges 0.5 % for currency exchange. How many euros do you pay just to convert?
u33l2-2.explanation: 2,000 × 0.005 = €10. And you'd pay again when you sell.

u33l2-3.prompt: A broker charges 0.2 % a year for custody. You have €20,000. How much do you pay per year?
u33l2-3.explanation: 20,000 × 0.002 = €40 a year, whether your portfolio goes up or down.

u33l2-4.prompt: Match each fee with what it charges for.
u33l2-4.explanation: Look at all of them, not just the one they advertise in big letters.
right: Converting euros into another currency
Not trading for a while
Holding your securities
Every time you buy or sell

u33l2-5.prompt: What's usually the biggest hidden cost when buying shares in another currency?
u33l2-5.explanation: From 0.1 % to 0.5 % or more per trade, and sometimes it isn't on the home page.

u33l2-6.prompt: Ana puts in €100 a month. Broker A charges a flat €3 per purchase; broker B, 0.5 % with no minimum. Which one works out cheaper for her?
options: B: it costs her €0.50 per purchase
u33l2-6.explanation: The fee that suits you best depends on the size of your purchases.
feedback: Exactly: €6 a year versus €36. With a one-off purchase of €10,000, though, A would win (€3 versus €50).

u33l2-7.prompt: If a broker advertises «€0 commission», investing with it costs nothing at all.
u33l2-7.explanation: It may charge for currency exchange, the spread or custody, or make money in other ways.

u33l2-8.prompt: Paid per trade or every year?
u33l2-8.explanation: Per-trade costs punish trading a lot; annual ones punish holding something expensive.
right: On every trade
Every year

u33l2-9.prompt: Quick: where do you find the annual cost (TER) of a fund or ETF?
options: In the KID, the key information document
u33l2-9.explanation: It's mandatory and standardised so you can compare.

u33l2-10.prompt: One-off purchase of €100. Order from cheapest to most expensive.
u33l2-10.explanation: With small amounts, flat fees weigh very heavily.

u33l3-1.prompt: What is payment for order flow (PFOF)?
options: What a market maker pays the broker to send it your orders
A fee you pay the broker
u33l3-1.explanation: That's why a broker can advertise €0 trading and still make money from your orders.

u33l3-2.prompt: In the EU, payment for order flow for retail clients is banned, with a temporary exception that ended on 30 June 2026.
u33l3-2.explanation: It's set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/791, which amended MiFIR.

u33l3-3.prompt: In what ways can a «commission-free» neobroker make money? Select all that apply.
options: By lending your shares to others
By giving money away to its customers
With the interest on cash it doesn't pay you anything on
u33l3-3.explanation: And also with subscriptions, spreads and products like crypto or CFDs.

u33l3-4.prompt: Pablo's app sends him notifications, confetti on every purchase and «streak» challenges. He's already trading 40 times a month. What would you suggest he think about?
options: That the design is pushing him to trade more than his plan needs
That he should keep going: if the app rewards him, he must be doing it right
That he should switch to another app with more rewards
u33l3-4.explanation: Gamification serves the broker's business, not necessarily your plan.
feedback: Good: a long-term plan doesn't need 40 trades a month.
The app rewards trading, not winning. The more you trade, the more costs you rack up.
More rewards, more nudges to trade.

u33l3-5.prompt: Does the neobroker earn more if you trade a lot, or does it earn even if you don't trade?
options: Interest on cash it doesn't pay you anything on
u33l3-5.explanation: Knowing where its income comes from tells you what behaviour it'll encourage.
right: Earns more if you trade a lot
Earns even if you don't trade

u33l3-6.prompt: Pablo trades 40 times a month, €500 each time, and loses 0.2 % on the spread per trade. How much does it cost him a year?
u33l3-6.explanation: 500 × 0.2 % = €1 per trade × 40 × 12 = €480 a year, even though the app says «€0 commission».

u33l3-7.prompt: If trading is free for you, the broker isn't making money from you.
u33l3-7.explanation: It makes money in other ways: currency, spread, interest, securities lending or subscriptions.

u33l3-8.prompt: Payment for order ____ is what a market maker pays the broker to send it your orders.

u33l3-9.prompt: What should you check about a neobroker before anything else?
options: That it's authorised and which compensation scheme protects you
That it gives you more confetti
u33l3-9.explanation: It's a firm like any other: safety first.

u33l3-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Brilliant! The more you trade, the more you learn
Look at how the app makes money and whether those 8 purchases were in your plan
Turn on the crypto alerts too
u33l3-10.explanation: An app can be cheap and at the same time push you to trade too much.
feedback: More trades usually means more costs and more impulsive decisions.
Nice! «Free» is almost never free, and notifications aren't a plan.
lines: I've downloaded a really cool investing app 😍
It's all free and it sends me alerts about shares that are going up. I've made 8 purchases today!

u33l4-1.prompt: Match each way of investing with its description.
u33l4-1.explanation: A robo-adviser is automated discretionary management and, usually, index-based.
right: You choose and buy your own index funds
A manager picks stocks to beat the index
You hand the decisions over to an authorised firm
Automatic index fund portfolio based on a test

u33l4-2.prompt: What does a robo-adviser do after your profile test?
options: It assigns you an index fund portfolio and rebalances it for you
u33l4-2.explanation: It automates the allocation, the contributions and the rebalancing.

u33l4-3.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years with the market at 7 % (an example). With a robo-adviser at 0.6 % in total you end up with about €64,306; doing it yourself at 0.2 %, about €71,968. How much does the convenience cost?
u33l4-3.explanation: 71,968 − 64,306 = €7,662. It's only worth it if it saves you from mistakes that would cost more.

u33l4-4.prompt: A robo-adviser removes the risk of your portfolio falling.
u33l4-4.explanation: It diversifies and rebalances, but if the market falls, your portfolio falls.

u33l4-5.prompt: Laura has no time, never remembers to rebalance and in 2022 she sold in the middle of a crash. She's torn between a robo-adviser and building her own index portfolio. What makes more sense?
options: Building it herself: it's cheaper, end of story
The robo-adviser could be worth it if it helps her avoid repeating those mistakes
u33l4-5.explanation: Cost matters, but behavioural mistakes can cost even more.
feedback: More expensive than both options and, on average, worse than its index.
Cheaper on paper, but her past mistakes cost her more than the fee would.
Good: she pays a bit more in exchange for automatic discipline. The key is not to abandon it during a crash.

u33l4-6.prompt: Is it an advantage of a robo-adviser or of doing it yourself?
options: You don't have to decide which funds to buy
It takes away the temptation to tinker with your portfolio
u33l4-6.explanation: Convenience and discipline versus cost and control.
right: Robo-adviser advantage
Do-it-yourself advantage

u33l4-7.prompt: In Spain, a robo-adviser has to be a firm authorised by the CNMV.
u33l4-7.explanation: Managing portfolios is a regulated investment service.

u33l4-8.prompt: What should you look at before signing up to a robo-adviser? Select all that apply.
options: Which funds it uses and how it rebalances
That it promises the highest return
The total cost: management plus funds
That it's authorised by the CNMV

u33l4-9.prompt: The questionnaire that measures your knowledge, goals and risk tolerance before managing your money is called the ____ test.
u33l4-9.explanation: The EU's MiFID rules require it for advice and portfolio management.

u33l4-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Neither, a bank fund with a manager is better
It depends: if you'll be consistent, doing it yourself is cheaper; if not, the robot helps you not slip up
Robo-adviser, always: robots don't make mistakes
u33l4-10.explanation: There's no single answer: cost versus discipline.
feedback: It's usually the most expensive option and, on average, returns less than its index.
That's it! Compare the extra cost with the mistakes it would save you from.
Robots follow rules, but the market can still fall. And they charge for the service.
lines: Should I get a robo-adviser or do it myself? 🤖
I don't want to be glued to the stock market.
